title: Judaism: blessings
hookLine: a blessing for bread, for thunder, for a rainbow: noticing through words

cards: Thunder rolls over the house. The usual response: a flinch, a look out the window, maybe the weather app. Now suppose the first response, before any of that, was a sentence.
A short, fixed sentence learned for exactly this moment. Another for the first rainbow after the storm. Another for the first bite of bread.

Another for new shoes, or seeing the ocean after a long time away. Your whole day would be stitched with small sentences, each one a way of noticing. In Jewish life, there really is a sentence for all of these.

teach.h: BLESSED ARE YOU, RULER OF THE UNIVERSE.
teach.b: Bracha, blessing. A standard blessing opens with fixed words: baruch atah Adonai, eloheinu melech ha-olam. Blessed are you, Lord our God, ruler of the universe.
Then comes the ending that fits the moment.
Before bread: who brings forth bread from the earth. That's the blessing called hamotzi. For thunder: whose strength and might fill the world.

For a rainbow: who remembers the covenant and keeps the promise, a nod back to Noah, and to brit, the covenant, from a few days ago. Why bless before eating something you already have? The Talmud gives a sharp answer.
It quotes a psalm, in the King James words, "The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof," and reasons that enjoying anything from the world without a blessing is like taking what isn't yours.
The blessing is a kind of asking permission and a kind of thank-you, at once. There's even a goal.
The Talmud records a teaching of Rabbi Meir that a person should say a hundred blessings every day. The daily prayers, the meals and the moments are how an observant day can add up to it.
A blessing makes you stop and name the thing. You can't bless bread you haven't noticed. You can't bless thunder while scrolling past it.
The fixed words do the noticing for you, until noticing becomes a habit.

how: Observant Jews say a bracha before and after eating and at many moments of the day, from waking to seeing lightning or a rainbow, and many aim for a hundred blessings daily.

games.q: you're about to eat bread you already own. why would a blessing come first?
o: because the earth is the LORD's: it's a way of asking and thanking.
games.why: the Talmud quotes Psalm 24: the earth is the LORD's. the blessing turns taking into receiving.

practice: Pick something plain, a cup of water, the chair holding you, the light through the window, and look at it properly, as if it were new.
If you pray, you can say the traditional opening, blessed are you; if you don't, simply name it slowly: this water, this chair, this light. Let the naming be the thank-you.

wordCard.voice: Bracha. A blessing: a fixed sentence that begins blessed are you, and turns bread, thunder and rainbows into moments noticed. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: blessing; baruch, blessed, shares the root.

carryVoice: Your line: blessed is. Two words, and the ordinary gets noticed. Two hundred fifty days now.
